analysis:
Integration review of the fast-reconnect PR. Production changes are small: CoordinatorClient.swift adds an injectable reconnectPolicy at init. CoordinatorClientState.swift:509-536 adds CoordinatorSessionRecorder, which holds only openedAt and closeCode behind an unfair lock. Connection.swift records the coordinator's close code. sentCloseCode bounds-checks content.count >= 2 and reads from the payload only when Network.framework reports noStatusReceived. CoordinatorReconnectPolicy.swift: close code 1012 gives a 0-1 s random wait without growing the backoff, and a session open 60 s or more after register resets the backoff. The rest of the PR is docs, a changelog and tests (MockCoordinator.dropActiveWebSocket gains a closeCode argument and keeps the 1001 default).

The supplied evidence shows no regression to TB-002, TB-011, T-053 or T-057. The close code comes from the trusted coordinator over TLS, and it only paces reconnection. It never feeds authorization. Docs and changelog state that every reconnect sends a fresh register and that cancellation and teardown of the old connection are unchanged. The defer teardown clears the capacity session and the App Attest resume nonce; the nonce is regenerated per connection. The log line adds only a numeric code.

Residual availability question (TB-002): a 0-1 s wait with no backoff growth on 1012 could create a coordinator reconnect storm. The same applies if the 60 s stable-session reset can be gamed by a peer that keeps sessions open just over 60 s. The wait is jittered and the coordinator is trusted, so this is a design tradeoff and not a vulnerability. Not verified because CoordinatorReconnectPolicy.swift and runLoop were only partly visible (replay of 82 of 155 units): the exact bounds, nonzero floors for the other paths, and the lock and ordering between the receive callback and runLoop reading end(). A later pass should confirm the 60 s timer starts at the register frame and that a failed registration does not reset the backoff.
